body:
Abhinavagupta opens with a maṅgala invoking his parents — Mother of stainless art and new creation, Father of hidden splendor with five faces — promising the Tantrasāra as the plain-words distillation of the vast Tantrāloka, then enters the teaching: knowledge, not ritual, is liberation's cause, because it opposes ignorance, the cause of bondage. Ignorance is twofold — intellectual (doubt and wrong conviction) and personal (thought-natured, contracted; saṃsāra's root). Initiation can wash the personal kind, but initiation itself requires prior intellectual determination, so determinative knowledge comes first. Scripture alone fully authorizes, absorbing lesser revelations discriminatively. Own nature is one autonomous light — the same in all things, unbounded by place, time, or form — whose contraction is bondage (the atom) and whose expansion is freedom; autonomy itself is bliss, will, consciousness, knowledge, action. Re-manifestation runs sudden or gradual, with or without means — will, knowledge, action as the three approaches (śāmbhava/śākta/āṇava), and a fourth.

The passage moves in four steps, each building on the last. First, the epistemic diagnosis: bondage is not a thing but a not-knowing, and not-knowing has two seats — the intellect that cannot decide (doubt, wrong conviction) and the person whose awareness is pulled tight into thoughts. Initiation, which removes the personal kind, presupposes the intellectual kind's removal, so determinative knowledge is principal; practised, it finishes the other job too, since thought-practice ends in thought-free awareness. For what you are — awareness squeezed into thoughts, but light by nature — is Śiva already. So in every case, adopt knowledge that decides rightly about everything. Second, the authority claim: scripture that counts is Lord-spoken, since it takes whatever lesser books say, keeps it discriminatively, and out-argues the rest. Lesser revelations free you partway; only the Lord's word — five streams, ten, eighteen, eight and all their branches — frees altogether. Its essence runs pañcasrotas → ṣaḍardha → Mālinīvijaya, whose content no gathering can exhaust. Nobody is free, or frees, without the nature of things spelled out — only pure knowing does that. And since man's highest end stands on practised knowing, this book begins here to secure it. Third, the ontological core: own nature can only be light (what doesn't shine can't be what a thing is), and only one light (nothing alien enters light, so natures can't differ; place and time are themselves light), and autonomous (illuminedness needs another light; none exists) — hence all-pervading, eternal, every form and none. Autonomy is bliss; wonder, will; shining, consciousness; grasp, knowledge; fitting every form, action — really three powers (will, knowing, doing). Contracted, that light is the atom; free, it is Śiva. Fourth, the fourfold means previewed: sudden or gradual re-manifestation, with or without means — will, knowledge, action as the three approaches, plus a fourth.
terms: jñāna (knowledge, liberation's cause), ajñāna (ignorance, twofold: buddhigata + pauruṣa), mala (stain, saṃsāra's root), svabhāva (own nature = prakāśa), svātantrya (autonomy = ānanda), prakāśa (light = saṃvit), aṇu (atom = contracted self), samāveśa (immersion, threefold: śāmbhava/śākta/āṇava).
see_also: A02 (anupāya), A05 (āṇava), essay0 Q1 ("What is my own nature?"), spans TS1.4/TS9.2/TS21.1/TS22.1.
function: Opens the whole work: establishes the problem (ignorance), the authority (Lord-spoken scripture), the one reality (autonomous light), and the fourfold means that the next four ahnikas will teach.
local_context: First ahnika; follows the maṅgala (1.1–1.3); precedes A02 (anupāya, the means-less immersion).
boundary: Mala specifics deferred (malanirṇaye). Upāya details deferred to A02–A05. Mālinīvijaya's inexhaustibility is Abhinava's claim, not argued here. The maṅgala's parent-imagery is invocatory, not doctrinal.
